result.reading: Block 14 is the narrator's flat one-line answer to Theodore's claim in 13 that, left to himself, he would have quit the Academy long ago: whatever he wants, that exit is now closed to him for lack of means. It applies to him, in the negative, the page's recurring measure of privilege, which is what Agnes (3), Anna (10) and the kept Academicians (18) can permit themselves. It also inverts block 3, which opens the same way for Agnes. It launches the exposition of 15–19 (the cost of study, the grant and its card, the debt that only staying keeps from coming due, the fourth-circle point after which repayment is hopeless, the grim work outside), which block 20 then presents as the pause Agnes deliberately leaves for it.

elements.where: where the narrator says what now stands between Theodore and leaving the Academy
elements.what: In Ukrainian this reflexive phrase is the everyday idiom for whether one has the money, or the position, for something. Its literal make-up, a verb of permitting with a reflexive pronoun, points instead to self-permission. Context selects the idiom: blocks 15–17 at once explain the money. Training costs a fortune, a grant pays for study and living, and the endlessly growing debt stays harmless only while he remains, so walking out would bring it down on him. Read literally, the barrier becomes self-discipline or a ban. That jars with his own line in 13 that, left to himself, he would have gone long ago, and leaves the reader wondering who or what is holding him back.

checks.ask: Does the translation avoid turning the barrier to leaving into self-restraint or a prohibition?
checks.fail: The wording has Theodore holding himself back, refusing himself, not daring, or not being permitted to leave.

elements.where: where the narrator says that leaving the Academy is now beyond Theodore
elements.what: This is the fourth use on the page of a single measure of privilege: what a person's money or rank entitles them to. Agnes has her flamboyant clothes in defiance of the dress code (3). Anna can do anything at all without her fate changing (10). The accredited Academicians kept by Seraph have their poetry and metaphysics (18). Block 3 opens with the same contrastive word followed by the same formula, so 14 reads as its negative image: the curator can flout the rules, while the student cannot even walk away. Heard as a refrain, it puts Theodore at the bottom of that scale and prepares 17's point that in Seraph nothing comes free, not even quitting.

checks.ask: Is leaving still presented as something Theodore can or cannot permit himself, the same measure applied to Agnes (3), Anna (10) and the Academicians (18), rather than stated as a bare inability?
checks.fail: The notion is gone: Theodore simply cannot leave, has no option or way out, is stuck or trapped, or leaving is called impossible. A rendering that keeps the notion but reads it as self-restraint is judged at E1, not here.

elements.where: in the narrator's statement that Theodore cannot leave the Academy, the part that says this was not always so
elements.what: This marks a change of state: there was a time when he could have quit, and it has passed. Block 18 gives the timing: a mage can earn a living from the second circle, but from the fourth the hope of repaying the debt is gone. Curators are assigned at the end of the fourth circle (3), so Theodore, who has one, is already past that point. The marker also answers his own line in 13 that he would have left well before now: the way out existed and has closed. Without it, his bind reads as a permanent fact of poverty rather than a trap that shut as he advanced, and 18 and 20 (the prospects of someone thrown out before the fifth circle) lose their setup.

checks.ask: Does the translation say that his inability to leave is new, so that leaving was once open to him and has stopped being so?
checks.fail: The inability is stated as plain and timeless, with nothing signalling that it used to be otherwise.
